self_contained_problem:
For an odd prime $p$ and an integer $a$ coprime to $p$, let $\left(\frac{a}{p}\right)$ denote the Legendre symbol. For nonnegative integers $k$, write the multinomial coefficient
$$\binom{4k}{k,k,k,k} = \frac{(4k)!}{(k!)^4}.$$
Prove or disprove the following three statements.

(a) For every prime $p > 3$ with $p \neq 11$,
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1} \frac{1}{15842^{k}}\binom{4k}{k,k,k,k} \equiv \begin{cases} 4x^{2} - 2p \pmod{p^{2}} & \text{if } \left(\tfrac{-11}{p}\right) = \left(\tfrac{2}{p}\right) = 1 \text{ and } p = x^{2} + 22y^{2}, \\ 2p - 8x^{2} \pmod{p^{2}} & \text{if } \left(\tfrac{-11}{p}\right) = \left(\tfrac{2}{p}\right) = -1 \text{ and } p = 2x^{2} + 11y^{2}, \\ 0 \pmod{p^{2}} & \text{if } \left(\tfrac{-11}{p}\right) = -\left(\tfrac{2}{p}\right). \end{cases}$$

(b) For every prime $p > 3$ with $p \neq 11$,
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1} \frac{280k + 19}{15842^{k}}\binom{4k}{k,k,k,k} \equiv 19\, p\,\left(\tfrac{-2}{p}\right) \pmod{p^{3}}.$$

(c) For every integer $n \geq 2$, the rational number
$$a_{n} := \frac{1}{2n(2n+1)\binom{2n}{n}}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(280k + 19)\binom{4k}{k,k,k,k}\, 15842^{\,2(n-1-k)}$$
is an integer, with the single exception that when $2n + 1$ is a power of $3$ one has $a_{n} \notin \mathbb{Z}$ but $3a_{n} \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $3a_{n} \notin 3\mathbb{Z}$.

self_contained_problem:
Let P be a simple polygon in the plane with vertex set V. The visibility graph G = (V, E) of P is the graph in which two vertices u, v ∈ V are adjacent if and only if the closed segment uv lies in the closure of P (so, in particular, all edges of the boundary of P are edges of G, and the boundary forms a Hamiltonian cycle of G). A hidden set (independent set) in G is a subset S ⊆ V such that no two vertices of S are adjacent in G; equivalently, no two vertices of S see each other inside P. 

Devise an algorithm that, given as input the visibility graph G together with the distinguished Hamiltonian cycle of G that corresponds to the boundary of P, computes a hidden set of G of maximum cardinality. In particular, determine the computational complexity of this problem and, if possible, give a polynomial-time exact algorithm or prove hardness.

self_contained_problem:
Let $m$ and $n$ be natural numbers, and let $(a_k)_{k\ge 1}$ be an arithmetic progression of real numbers with first term $a_1$ and common difference $d$, so that $a_k = a_1 + (k-1)d$ for every natural number $k$. Suppose that
$$a_m = \frac{1}{n} \qquad \text{and} \qquad a_n = \frac{1}{m}.$$
Prove each of the following:

(a) $a_1 = d$, i.e. the first term equals the common difference.

(b) For every natural number $t$, the term indexed by $tmn$ satisfies
$$a_{tmn} = t.$$

(c) Let $S_N = \sum_{k=1}^{N} a_k$ denote the sum of the first $N$ terms. Then for every natural number $t$,
$$S_{tmn} = \frac{(mn+1)\,t}{2}.$$

self_contained_problem:
Let $g$ be a smooth Riemannian metric on the two-dimensional torus $T^2 = \mathbb{R}^2/\mathbb{Z}^2$, and let $\phi_t : TT^2 \to TT^2$ denote its geodesic flow. A smooth function $F : TT^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ is called a first integral of the geodesic flow if $F \circ \phi_t = F$ for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$. We say $F$ is polynomial of degree $n$ in the velocities if, in any local coordinate chart $(x^1,x^2)$ with induced fiber coordinates $(v^1,v^2)$ on $TT^2$, $F$ is a homogeneous polynomial of degree $n$ in $(v^1,v^2)$ with coefficients depending smoothly on $(x^1,x^2)$. Equivalently, such an $F$ corresponds to a symmetric Killing tensor field of rank $n$ on $(T^2,g)$. The Hamiltonian $H(x,v) = \tfrac{1}{2}g_{ij}(x)v^i v^j$ is itself a polynomial integral of degree $2$. A Killing vector field is a vector field $X$ on $T^2$ whose flow consists of isometries of $g$, equivalently a rank-$1$ Killing tensor; existence of such a (nontrivial) $X$ produces a linear-in-velocity integral $g_{ij}X^i v^j$.

Prove or disprove the following statement: if the geodesic flow of $(T^2,g)$ admits a first integral that is polynomial of degree $3$ in the velocities and is functionally independent of the Hamiltonian $H$, then $g$ admits a nontrivial Killing vector field (equivalently, the cubic integral is reducible to lower-degree integrals built from $H$ and a linear integral).
